summary: Presents four YANG 1.1 modules, three IETF ones (ietf-tls-common, ietf-tls-client, ietf-tls-server) and one supporting IANA module. The client and server modules support configuring and monitoring TLS endpoints, and the groupings are meant to be reused by models for protocols that run over TLS.

eli5.summary: TLS is the lock that keeps web traffic private. This gives a standard form for writing down how each side of that lock should be set up, so different tools can share the same form.

subtitle: Reusable YANG building blocks for configuring the TLS client and TLS server inside any management data model.

tldr.problem: Many management models need to configure a TLS client or server, and each would otherwise define its own way to describe identities, trusted peers, TLS versions and cipher suites.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9645 defines three IETF YANG modules (ietf-tls-common, ietf-tls-client, ietf-tls-server) with groupings that other models import, plus a script IANA used to build an iana-tls-cipher-suite-algs module from its TLS Cipher Suites registry.
tldr.outcome: Models for HTTPS and for NETCONF over TLS can share one definition of TLS settings. The groupings cover only TLS itself, so ports and addresses come from a transport-level module such as RFC 9643.

today: RFC 9645 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Provides
sections.content:
RFC 9645 presents four YANG 1.1 modules: three IETF modules and one supporting IANA module. The IETF modules are ietf-tls-common, ietf-tls-client and ietf-tls-server. The client and server modules are the primary productions, supporting the configuration and monitoring of TLS clients and servers. The IANA module is iana-tls-cipher-suite-algs, which defines YANG enumerations for an IANA-maintained algorithm registry.

The modules define groupings, reusable chunks of a data model. The text calls them "generic", meaning "least common denominator" rather than "complete": basic TLS support is included and advanced features are left to augmentations made by consuming modules.

The groupings are meant for applications that configure TLS client and server protocol stacks. The RFC names two uses: the data models for HTTPS and for clients and servers using NETCONF over TLS.
sections.eli5: It is a kit of ready-made pieces for writing down TLS settings. The basic pieces are included, and anyone who needs extras can add them.

sections.title: Where These Modules Fit
sections.content:
The TLS groupings belong to a family of RFCs that together support configuring clients and servers of the NETCONF and RESTCONF protocols. The RFC's dependency diagram labels them crypto-types (RFC 9640), truststore (RFC 9641), keystore (RFC 9642), tcp-client-server (RFC 9643), ssh-client-server (RFC 9644) and tls-client-server (this document).

The TLS modules deliberately avoid transport-level configuration, such as which ports to listen on or connect to, leaving that to a module like the one in RFC 9643. This lets an application choose how the TCP connection is made. NETCONF Call Home (RFC 8071) is the example: it can use tls-server-grouping for the TLS parts and add its own call-home nodes.

The document is compliant with the Network Management Datastore Architecture.
sections.eli5: This RFC handles only the lock part of the connection. Another RFC handles where the connection goes.

sections.title: Common TLS Settings
sections.content:
The ietf-tls-common module holds what clients and servers share. Its hello-params-grouping has a tls-versions container with a min and a max version, and an ordered cipher-suites list. If several are permitted, the algorithm that appears first in the client list and is also permitted by the server is the one used.

Both TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) and TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) can be configured. The RFC notes that TLS 1.2 is obsoleted by TLS 1.3 but is still in common use, so its feature statement is marked status deprecated. To cover both versions, the permitted algorithms should include TLS Cipher Suites, TLS SignatureScheme and TLS Supported Groups.

The module has five features: tls12, tls13, hello-params, asymmetric-key-pair-generation and supported-algorithms. As in the SSH sibling document, it also defines a read-only supported-algorithms container for discovery and a generate-asymmetric-key-pair RPC.
sections.eli5: You can say which lock designs you accept, newest and oldest, and rank them. Both sides compare lists and use the first one they both like.

sections.title: The Client and Server Groupings
sections.content:
The tls-client-grouping has a client-identity that is optional, because client authentication MAY occur at a higher protocol layer. When set, it picks one credential type: a certificate, a raw private key, a TLS 1.2 pre-shared key, or a TLS 1.3 external pre-shared key (tls13-epsk). server-authentication holds the trust anchors: CA certificates, end-entity certificates, raw public keys, and flags for TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 pre-shared keys. hello-params reuses the common settings, and keepalives tests whether the server is still alive at the TLS protocol layer.

The tls-server-grouping mirrors this. server-identity picks a certificate, a raw private key, or one of the two pre-shared key kinds. client-authentication is optional and sets trust anchors for checking clients. hello-params and keepalives follow. The server keepalives let the TLS client test the server, and also hold a presence container to test the client.

Each credential type is enabled by its own feature, for example client-ident-raw-public-key or server-auth-x509-cert. Keys and trust anchors come from the keystore (RFC 9642) and truststore (RFC 9641) groupings. Neither module defines protocol-accessible nodes of its own.
sections.eli5: The client form asks which ID the client shows and who it trusts. The server form asks which ID the server shows and which visitors it accepts. Each has a box for checking the other side is still there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The three IETF modules define groupings and will not be deployed as standalone modules, so their security implications depend on how other modules use them. Designers who import the groupings must do their own analysis.

The data is meant to be reached through YANG management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF, which have mandatory-to-implement secure transports and mutual authentication, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) restricts what each user may do.

All writable nodes in the client and server modules have the NACM extension default-deny-write, since changing a key or a reference to a key may dramatically alter the security policy. The server module relies on the key and private-key nodes from RFC 9640, which already have default-deny-all to block unrestricted reads of cleartext keys.

The generate-asymmetric-key-pair RPC can return a private key in cleartext when that feature is enabled and requested. The RFC says it is NOT RECOMMENDED for private keys to pass the server's security perimeter.
sections.eli5: Settings that could weaken the lock cannot be changed by just anyone, and secret keys are not handed out to people who only ask to look.

sections.title: The IANA Cipher Suite Module
sections.content:
The iana-tls-cipher-suite-algs module turns the IANA "TLS Cipher Suites" registry into YANG enumerations. IANA used the script in Appendix A to generate it, and the module is published and maintained by IANA, not by this RFC.

New values must not be added to the YANG module directly. They go into the registry, and a matching enum statement is then added to the module. A registry "Recommended" value of "N" maps to YANG status deprecated. There is no mapping to status obsolete, since the registry cannot express a logical "MUST NOT" recommendation. The RFC calls this unfortunate, given that single-DES and IDEA cipher suites were moved to Historic.

The RFC also asks IANA to register URIs in the IETF XML registry and the module names in the YANG Module Names registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of lock designs is kept by a librarian, and a script copies it into the form so the two always match.
